newsitem.title: USA: Alabama gov. may revive $700 mln highway bond bill.
newsitem.headline: Alabama gov. may revive $700 mln highway bond bill.

text.p: Alabama Gov. Fob James is revising part of his $700 million highway bond proposal and might resubmit it to the legislature in an August special session, a spokeswoman said Tuesday.

"He has said he would like to have that, along with the other two bond bills he introduced in the regular session but unless he has support for them, he will not introduce them into the special session," James' spokeswoman Sandra Nesbitt said.
In addition to the highway bonds, James proposed $80 million of general obligation bonds for parks and $150 million of bonds for public school computers and technology.
All three proposals stalled during the regular legislative session that ended May 19.

James tentatively plans to call lawmakers back in a special session on Aug. 18 to rework the $1 billion general fund budget and the $3.7 billion public eduction budget. James vetoed both on May 29, saying they contained too many "pork barrel" projects.

Like the original version, the new highway bond proposal would use existing gasoline taxes to pay debt service on the 20-year bonds. It would allocate $150 million for resurfacing roads and highways, $150 million for bridge repair and replacement and $81.9 million to be divided among the state's 67 counties for local projects, Nesbitt said.

The original bill also allocated $318 for construction of bypasses around Birmingham, Huntsville, Tuscaloosa, Decatur, Montgomery and Anniston, plus widening of several two-lane highways to four lanes.
Nesbitt said the revised version would replace some of those urban projects with construction of industrial access roads.

"There has been a real interest shown in making some industrial access road projects available that they had not had in the first one because of expanding industry and the economic impact that would have," Nesbitt said. "That has become an important part, but basically, aside from that, it would remain the same."

State Transportation Director Jimmy Butts said the new bill would put more emphasis on road projects identified in the state's five-year construction and repair plan, and less on distrectionary money for lawmakers' pet projects.
"We won't be playing 'Let's Make A Deal,'" Butts told reporters after meeting with the legislature's Joint Highway Committee on Monday.
